papers.core_contribution: Design choices, particularly molecular representation and tokenization, significantly affect the chemical interpretability of language models, with SMILES and atomwise tokenization yielding more chemically meaningful embeddings, even when downstream task performance is similar.
papers.conclusion: Design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented in language models, and SMILES with atomwise tokenization is favorable for interpretability, guiding future development of chemically grounded CLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Atomwise tokenization generally yields better downstream performance than SentencePiece tokenization.
SMILES representations produce more chemically structured latent spaces than SELFIES representations.
BART and RoBERTa architectures yield comparably interpretable representations, but BART embeddings are more linearly separable for certain molecular properties.
RoBERTa shows a stronger ability to distinguish between atom types than BART.
The choice of molecular representation has a greater impact on interpretability than the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring alternative molecular representations such as t-SMILES and DeepSMILES.
Comparing BART's generative capabilities with other large language model architectures like GPT.
Investigating the differences and synergies between large language models and graph-based approaches such as GROVER.
Utilizing highly curated datasets from specialized domains to reveal subtle chemical relationships.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical language models (CLMs) have shown strong performance in molecular property prediction and generation tasks. However, the impact of design choices, such as molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, and model architecture, on both performance and chemical interpretability remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically evaluate how these factors influence CLM performance and chemical understanding. We evaluated models through fine-tuning on downstream tasks and probing the structure of their latent spaces using simple classifiers and dimensionality reduction techniques.Despite similar performance on downstream tasks across model configurations, we observed substantial differences in the structure and interpretability of their internal representations. SMILES molecular representation format with atomwise tokenization strategy consistently produced more chemically meaningful embeddings, while models based on BART and RoBERTa architectures yielded comparably interpretable representations. These findings highlight that design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented, even when external metrics appear unchanged. This insight can inform future model development, encouraging more chemically grounded and interpretable CLMs.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: How are high-level human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs, and how does the sparsity of these representations vary with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse probing to localize individual neurons representing features in LLMs, revealing that early layers use superposition (sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons), middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons for higher-level features, and model scale increases representational sparsity with varied dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Sparse probing is a powerful tool for understanding feature representation in LLMs, revealing superposition in early layers and monosemantic neurons in middle layers, with scaling effects on sparsity, and opens many directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse linear combinations of polysemantic neurons.
Middle layers contain seemingly dedicated (monosemantic) neurons for higher-level contextual features like language or code.
Increasing model scale generally increases representational sparsity, but different features exhibit distinct scaling dynamics.
Sparse probing is an effective method for locating interpretable neurons, even when they are in superposition.
There is a tremendous amount of interpretable structure within the neurons of LLMs, accessible through careful probing and analysis.
papers.limitation:
Interpretation of neurons can be misleading due to 'interpretability illusions' from only examining maximum activating examples.
Conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
future_direction: Apply sparse probing to other model families and architectures.
Study the dynamics of feature representation during training, not just in final models.
Extend sparse probing to multimodal models and other modalities.
papers.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: TopK Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we build a language model architecture that enjoys the interpretability of sparse autoencoders without suffering the drawbacks of post-hoc training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TopK LMs, a transformer-based language model architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function to achieve inherent, SAE-like interpretability without requiring post-hoc training, while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: TopK LMs represent a significant advance toward trustworthy AI systems by making interpretability a built-in feature, demonstrating that performance and interpretability need not be competing objectives.
papers.key_findings:
TopK LMs achieve competitive language modeling and downstream task performance compared to dense baselines, with only a moderate increase in model size.
Neurons in TopK LMs exhibit higher concept specialization, as measured by lower token and semantic entropy, making them more interpretable.
Single-neuron interventions (activation patching) can causally steer the model's text generation towards specific concepts.
The formation and specialization of individual neurons can be traced continuously across training checkpoints and model layers.
Sparsity annealing during training improves convergence and model performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models up to ~1B parameters; effectiveness on significantly larger models remains an open question.
Evaluation focused on language modeling and standard reasoning benchmarks, leaving performance on specialized downstream tasks unclear.
Long-context modeling capabilities and the interaction between TopK sparsity and attention over long sequences were not examined.
The approach is currently limited to text-only models; extending to multimodal architectures requires future research.
Specific societal applications that could benefit from the model's interpretability were not explored.
future_direction: Scaling the TopK LM approach to significantly larger models (tens or hundreds of billions of parameters).
Extending TopK activation to multimodal architectures combining text with images, audio, or other modalities.
Investigating how TopK LMs can address concrete challenges in model alignment, fairness assessment, safety evaluation, and trustworthy AI deployment.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for analyzing and interpreting the activation space of transformer-based language models (LMs). However, SAEs suffer several shortcomings that diminish their utility and internal validity. Since SAEs are trained post-hoc, it is unclear if the failure to discover a particular concept is a failure on the SAE's side or due to the underlying LM not representing this concept. This problem is exacerbated by training conditions and architecture choices affecting which features an SAE learns. When tracing how LMs learn concepts during training, the lack of feature stability also makes it difficult to compare SAEs features across different checkpoints. To address these limitations, we introduce a modification to the transformer architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function at chosen layers, making the model's hidden states equivalent to the latent features of a TopK SAE. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc training while providing interpretability comparable to SAEs. The resulting TopK LMs offer a favorable trade-off between model size, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Despite this simple architectural change, TopK LMs maintain their original capabilities while providing robust interpretability benefits. Our experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations learned by TopK LMs enable successful steering through targeted neuron interventions and facilitate detailed analysis of neuron formation processes across checkpoints and layers. These features make TopK LMs stable and reliable tools for understanding how language models learn and represent concepts, which we believe will significantly advance future research on model interpretability and controllability.

papers.title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the Local Interaction Basis (LIB) method find interpretable and sparsely-interacting features in neural networks, particularly in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Local Interaction Basis (LIB), a method to transform neural network activations into a basis of computationally-relevant and sparsely-interacting features, and shows it works on toy models but not on language models.
papers.conclusion: LIB is promising on toy models but does not achieve interpretable and sparsely-interacting features on language models, likely due to the assumption of a linear non-overcomplete basis.
papers.key_findings:
LIB identifies more computationally-relevant features than PCA in modular addition and CIFAR-10 models.
LIB features interact more sparsely than PCA features in CIFAR-10 and some layers of language models.
LIB does not produce more interpretable features than PCA in language models.
Integrated gradient interaction graphs can aid circuit discovery in toy models.
LIB does not reveal modular structure in language models.
papers.limitation: LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models.
future_direction: Generalizing LIB to overcomplete bases to handle features in superposition.
Exploring other ways to average attributions over the dataset.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the behavior of neural networks by reverse-engineering their internal computations. However, current methods struggle to find clear interpretations of neural network activations because a decomposition of activations into computational features is missing. Individual neurons or model components do not cleanly correspond to distinct features or functions. We present a novel interpretability method that aims to overcome this limitation by transforming the activations of the network into a new basis - the Local Interaction Basis (LIB). LIB aims to identify computational features by removing irrelevant activations and interactions. Our method drops irrelevant activation directions and aligns the basis with the singular vectors of the Jacobian matrix between adjacent layers. It also scales features based on their importance for downstream computation, producing an interaction graph that shows all computationally-relevant features and interactions in a model. We evaluate the effectiveness of LIB on modular addition and CIFAR-10 models, finding that it identifies more computationally-relevant features that interact more sparsely, compared to principal component analysis. However, LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models. We conclude that LIB is a promising theory-driven approach for analyzing neural networks, but in its current form is not applicable to large language models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Low-$N$ Protein Function Prediction and Design
papers.research_question: How effective are sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for protein function prediction and design in low-data (low-N) regimes?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a compact and biologically meaningful latent space that improves low-N fitness prediction and enables effective protein design via latent steering, outperforming ESM2 baselines.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a powerful tool for low-N protein function prediction and design, expanding the biologist's toolkit for resource-constrained applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform ESM2 baselines in 58% of fitness extrapolation tasks with as few as 24 training sequences.
SAEs design top-fitness variants in 83% of cases via latent steering, compared to designing with ESM2 alone.
The sparse latent space of SAEs encodes biologically interpretable motifs and compresses relevant information, reducing overfitting in low-N regimes.
Analysis of steered variants reveals that SAEs activate latents corresponding to known biological motifs such as active sites, allosteric sites, and epistatic sites.
SAE performance is influenced by the number of available multiple sequence alignment (MSA) sequences for training.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to a set of proteins; it could be extended to other proteins with clinically relevant functions such as antibiotic resistance and viral replication.
SAE performance is strongly influenced by the number of MSA sequences available for training; strategies are needed for robust training when MSAs are shallow.
Protein engineering experiments rely on in-silico fitness models; wet lab validation is necessary to verify function.
Designed variants are constrained to a maximum of five mutations away from the wildtype; beyond this radius, designing highly-functional sequences is difficult with a single predictive latent.
In-silico evaluation tools become less reliable the further away variants are from the wildtype.
future_direction: Extend evaluation to other proteins with clinically relevant functions.
Explore strategies for robust SAE training when multiple sequence alignments are shallow or unavailable.
Couple SAE steering with physics-based tools like Rosetta to jointly optimize for both function and stability.
papers.abstract: Predicting protein function from amino acid sequence remains a central challenge in data-scarce (low-$N$) regimes, limiting machine learning-guided protein design when only small amounts of assay-labeled sequence-function data are available. Protein language models (pLMs) have advanced the field by providing evolutionary-informed embeddings and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have enabled decomposition of these embeddings into interpretable latent variables that capture structural and functional features. However, the effectiveness of SAEs for low-$N$ function prediction and protein design has not been systematically studied. Herein, we evaluate SAEs trained on fine-tuned ESM2 embeddings across diverse fitness extrapolation and protein engineering tasks. We show that SAEs, with as few as 24 sequences, consistently outperform or compete with their ESM2 baselines in fitness prediction, indicating that their sparse latent space encodes compact and biologically meaningful representations that generalize more effectively from limited data. Moreover, steering predictive latents exploits biological motifs in pLM representations, yielding top-fitness variants in 83% of cases compared to designing with ESM2 alone.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Finding the Translation Switch: Discovering and Exploiting the Task-Initiation Features in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanism within instruction-tuned models is responsible for the innate translation ability of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to identify 'translation initiation' features in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders and demonstrates their causal role; proposes a mechanistic data selection strategy for efficient fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The paper decodes the translation initiation features in LLMs and shows how mechanistic insights can be used for efficient fine-tuning and specialization.
papers.key_findings:
A small set of 'translation initiation' features are causally responsible for the model's translation ability.
Amplifying these features improves translation quality and reduces hallucinations across diverse language pairs.
These features are language-agnostic and generalize across different translation directions.
A data selection strategy that prioritizes 'mechanistically hard' samples (low activation of initiation features) improves fine-tuning efficiency and reduces hallucinations.
The identified mechanisms are transferable across scales within the same model family but not across different architectures.
papers.limitation: The translation initiation features are not transferable across different model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit strong translation abilities, even without task-specific fine-tuning. However, the internal mechanisms governing this innate capability remain largely opaque. To demystify this process, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and introduce a novel framework for identifying task-specific features. Our method first recalls features that are frequently co-activated on translation inputs and then filters them for functional coherence using a PCA-based consistency metric. This framework successfully isolates a small set of **translation initiation** features. Causal interventions demonstrate that amplifying these features steers the model towards correct translation, while ablating them induces hallucinations and off-task outputs, confirming they represent a core component of the model's innate translation competency. Moving from analysis to application, we leverage this mechanistic insight to propose a new data selection strategy for efficient fine-tuning. Specifically, we prioritize training on **mechanistically hard** samples-those that fail to naturally activate the translation initiation features. Experiments show this approach significantly improves data efficiency and suppresses hallucinations. Furthermore, we find these mechanisms are transferable to larger models of the same family. Our work not only decodes a core component of the translation mechanism in LLMs but also provides a blueprint for using internal model mechanism to create more robust and efficient models. The codes are available at https://github.com/flamewei123/AAAI26-translation-Initiation-Features.

papers.title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: Towards Uncovering How Large Language Model Works: An Explainability Perspective
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques uncover the internal mechanisms of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a systematic overview of existing explainability techniques, including mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering, to uncover the inner workings of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that explainability techniques like mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering are crucial for understanding LLMs, but there are still challenges such as scalability and evaluation of explanations.
papers.limitation: The survey does not explore the complete landscape of relevant XAI methods for understanding LLMs, due to space constraints.
future_direction: Developing scalable techniques to analyze and interpret the intricate knowledge structures embedded within LLMs.
Revealing the intricate mechanisms that give rise to advanced reasoning capabilities in LLMs.
Fully leveraging insights from explainability to develop techniques that can substantially improve LLM performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have led to breakthroughs in language tasks, yet the internal mechanisms that enable their remarkable generalization and reasoning abilities remain opaque. This lack of transparency presents challenges such as hallucinations, toxicity, and misalignment with human values, hindering the safe and beneficial deployment of LLMs. This paper aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying LLM functionality through the lens of explainability. First, we review how knowledge is architecturally composed within LLMs and encoded in their internal parameters via mechanistic interpretability techniques. Then, we summarize how knowledge is embedded in LLM representations by leveraging probing techniques and representation engineering. Additionally, we investigate the training dynamics through a mechanistic perspective to explain phenomena such as grokking and memorization. Lastly, we explore how the insights gained from these explanations can enhance LLM performance through model editing, improve efficiency through pruning, and better align with human values.

papers.title: Capturing Polysemanticity with PRISM: A Multi-Concept Feature Description Framework
papers.research_question: How can we capture polysemanticity (multiple concepts per feature) in large language models to improve automated feature description methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISM, a framework for generating multi-concept feature descriptions that captures polysemanticity in LLMs, outperforming single-concept methods in description quality and faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: PRISM provides a more nuanced and accurate understanding of feature polysemanticity in LLMs, advancing automated interpretability by moving beyond single-concept descriptions.
papers.key_findings:
PRISM (max) achieves higher AUROC and MAD scores than existing feature description methods across multiple models and feature types.
PRISM reveals that individual features often encode a diverse set of concepts, demonstrating polysemanticity.
The degree of polysemanticity varies across model layers and architectures, with no consistent trend with depth.
Neuron-based features (MLP) are generally more interpretable than SAE-based features from the residual stream.
The framework is robust to variations in clustering parameters and the choice of language model for description generation.
papers.limitation: Relies on the quality of clustering and the language model used for description generation, which may produce unfaithful explanations.
future_direction: Extending PRISM to other modalities, such as vision or multimodal models.
Investigating the relationship between polysemanticity and model performance.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability research aims to identify concepts encoded in neural network features to enhance human understanding of model behavior. Within the context of large language models (LLMs) for natural language processing (NLP), current automated neuron-level feature description methods face two key challenges: limited robustness and the assumption that each neuron encodes a single concept (monosemanticity), despite increasing evidence of polysemanticity. This assumption restricts the expressiveness of feature descriptions and limits their ability to capture the full range of behaviors encoded in model internals. To address this, we introduce Polysemantic FeatuRe Identification and Scoring Method (PRISM), a novel framework specifically designed to capture the complexity of features in LLMs. Unlike approaches that assign a single description per neuron, common in many automated interpretability methods in NLP, PRISM produces more nuanced descriptions that account for both monosemantic and polysemantic behavior. We apply PRISM to LLMs and, through extensive benchmarking against existing methods, demonstrate that our approach produces more accurate and faithful feature descriptions, improving both overall description quality (via a description score) and the ability to capture distinct concepts when polysemanticity is present (via a polysemanticity score).

papers.title: REMA: A Unified Reasoning Manifold Framework for Interpreting Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we understand and localize reasoning failures in Large Language Models by analyzing the geometric structure of their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of the 'Reasoning Manifold' and the REMA framework, which diagnoses reasoning failures by quantifying and localizing the geometric deviation of erroneous internal representations from the manifold formed by correct ones.
papers.conclusion: REMA provides a novel geometric perspective for interpreting LLM reasoning, demonstrating that deviations from a 'Reasoning Manifold' are indicative of errors and allowing for the localization of failure points within the model's inference path.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states of both correct and incorrect reasoning exhibit low-dimensional structures (low Intrinsic Dimension).
Representations of erroneous reasoning consistently show statistically significant geometric deviation from the manifold of correct reasoning.
These deviations can be traced back to specific model layers (divergence points), revealing model- and task-dependent patterns of failure origins.
The relative deviation distance is negatively correlated with model accuracy, suggesting more difficult tasks lead to larger deviations.
Correct and error reasoning representations are highly separable in the latent space, as shown by UMAP/t-SNE visualizations and classifier accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The manifold approximation depends on the diversity and density of the correct samples.
Binary partitioning of samples into 'correct' and 'error' based on exact text match might misclassify 'nearly correct' reasoning.
future_direction: Building more precise manifold models using advanced manifold learning techniques.
Investigating the fundamental reasons for the formation of reasoning manifolds.
Exploring more fine-grained, confidence-based, or soft-scoring-based partitioning methods.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform complex reasoning and their failure mechanisms is a challenge in interpretability research. To provide a measurable geometric analysis perspective, we define the concept of the Reasoning Manifold, a latent low-dimensional geometric structure formed by the internal representations corresponding to all correctly reasoned generations. This structure can be conceptualized as the embodiment of the effective thinking paths that the model has learned to successfully solve a given task. Based on this concept, we build REMA, a framework that explains the origins of failures by quantitatively comparing the spatial relationships of internal model representations corresponding to both erroneous and correct reasoning samples. Specifically, REMA first quantifies the geometric deviation of each erroneous representation by calculating its k-nearest neighbors distance to the approximated manifold formed by correct representations, thereby providing a unified failure signal. It then localizes the divergence points where these deviations first become significant by tracking this deviation metric across the model's layers and comparing it against a baseline of internal fluctuations from correct representations, thus identifying where the reasoning chain begins to go off-track. Our extensive experiments on diverse language and multimodal models and tasks demonstrate the low-dimensional nature of the reasoning manifold and the high separability between erroneous and correct reasoning representations. The results also validate the effectiveness of the REMA framework in analyzing the origins of reasoning failures. This research connects abstract reasoning failures to measurable geometric deviations in representations, providing new avenues for in-depth understanding and diagnosis of the internal computational processes of black-box models.

papers.title: Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do features in language models emerge and evolve internally during pre-training? What is the internal dynamics of model pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using cross-snapshot crosscoders to track the evolution of interpretable features during language model pre-training, revealing a two-phase learning process (statistical then feature learning) and establishing causal connections between feature formation and downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that cross-snapshot crosscoders can successfully track fine-grained feature evolution during pre-training, providing empirical evidence for a statistical-to-feature-learning phase transition and opening possibilities for detailed analysis of representation learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Feature evolution follows a two-phase pattern: a statistical learning phase followed by a feature learning phase, with most features beginning to form around step 1000.
Decoder norms of crosscoder features serve as effective proxies for tracking feature strength and presence across training snapshots.
More complex features (e.g., induction, context-sensitive) tend to emerge later in training than simpler features (e.g., previous token).
Attribution-based circuit tracing shows that the formation of specific crosscoder features causally contributes to improvements on downstream tasks like subject-verb agreement.
Features undergo a universal directional shift around step 1000, after which they rotate more gradually while maintaining similarity to their post-step 1000 orientations.
papers.limitation: Crosscoders may theoretically misalign unrelated features or split shared features across snapshots, though the authors argue these are rare in practice.
papers.abstract: Language models obtain extensive capabilities through pre-training. However, the pre-training process remains a black box. In this work, we track linear interpretable feature evolution across pre-training snapshots using a sparse dictionary learning method called crosscoders. We find that most features begin to form around a specific point, while more complex patterns emerge in later training stages. Feature attribution analyses reveal causal connections between feature evolution and downstream performance. Our feature-level observations are highly consistent with previous findings on Transformer's two-stage learning process, which we term a statistical learning phase and a feature learning phase. Our work opens up the possibility to track fine-grained representation progress during language model learning dynamics.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and steerability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by incorporating user-specified concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE), a framework that prunes low-utility SAE neurons and augments the latent space with a concept bottleneck aligned to user-defined concepts, improving interpretability and steerability.
papers.conclusion: CB-SAE unifies sparse autoencoders with concept bottleneck models, enabling robust interpretation and control of vision representations across modalities and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE neurons have low interpretability or steerability, rendering them ineffective for downstream use.
SAEs often fail to represent user-specified concepts, limiting their practical utility.
CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% over SAE baselines across LVLMs and image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) promise a unified approach for mechanistic interpretability, concept discovery, and model steering in LLMs and LVLMs. However, realizing this potential requires that the learned features be both interpretable and steerable. To that end, we introduce two new computationally inexpensive interpretability and steerability metrics and conduct a systematic analysis on LVLMs. Our analysis uncovers two observations; (i) a majority of SAE neurons exhibit either low interpretability or low steerability or both, rendering them ineffective for downstream use; and (ii) due to the unsupervised nature of SAEs, user-desired concepts are often absent in the learned dictionary, thus limiting their practical utility. To address these limitations, we propose Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE) - a novel post-hoc framework that prunes low-utility neurons and augments the latent space with a lightweight concept bottleneck aligned to a user-defined concept set. The resulting CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% across LVLMs and image generation tasks. We will make our code and model weights available.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Explaining Language Models' Predictions with High-Impact Concepts
papers.research_question: How to derive reliable explanations for language model predictions by extracting high-impact concepts that cause substantial changes in predictions, as opposed to correlational features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces HI-Concept, a framework for extracting high-impact concepts from language models to explain predictions, which optimizes for causal impact and provides both global and local explanations.
papers.conclusion: HI-Concept provides impactful, counterfactual, and user-friendly explanations for language models, setting a foundation for causal NLP explainability.
papers.key_findings:
HI-Concept discovers concepts with higher impact than baseline methods, as measured by I(C) and ∆Acc.
The method maintains faithfulness to the original model's predictions, with high recovering accuracy (RAcc).
Human studies show that HI-Concept identifies words that are more causal and understandable to humans.
The method is effective on both synthetic and real text classification datasets.
papers.limitation: HI-Concept only encourages high impact in post-hoc model explanations and should serve as an assistive tool instead of being accepted as ground-truth.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other domains such as vision or tabular tasks.
Use the causal objective to address spurious correlations during training.
papers.abstract: The emergence of large-scale pretrained language models has posed unprecedented challenges in deriving explanations of why the model has made some predictions. Stemmed from the compositional nature of languages, spurious correlations have further undermined the trustworthiness of NLP systems, leading to unreliable model explanations that are merely correlated with the output predictions. To encourage fairness and transparency, there exists an urgent demand for reliable explanations that allow users to consistently understand the model's behavior. In this work, we propose a complete framework for extending concept-based interpretability methods to NLP. Specifically, we propose a post-hoc interpretability method for extracting predictive high-level features (concepts) from the pretrained model's hidden layer activations. We optimize for features whose existence causes the output predictions to change substantially, \ie generates a high impact. Moreover, we devise several evaluation metrics that can be universally applied. Extensive experiments on real and synthetic tasks demonstrate that our method achieves superior results on {predictive impact}, usability, and faithfulness compared to the baselines.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Steering Effectiveness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the reliability of activation-based steering in LLMs be diagnosed using internal model signals such as entropy and KL divergence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that internal mechanistic signals (NBF and KL divergence) can predict steering effectiveness and introduces rotation-based steering as a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods.
papers.conclusion: Internal mechanistic signals can predict steering effectiveness, and rotation-based steering provides a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods, making steering a more measurable and predictable process.
papers.key_findings:
LLM judges (ChatGPT-4o-mini and Gemini-Flash-2.5) show substantial agreement in evaluating steering outputs after correcting for calibration bias.
Effective steering is characterized by structured entropy preservation (NBF) and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps.
Internal signals (NBF, KL, attention patterns) can predict steering quality with reasonable accuracy.
Rotation-based steering outperforms naive additive steering in terms of steering-coherence trade-off.
Attention patterns show a drop in confidence immediately after the intervention layer, correlating with coherence.
papers.limitation:
Limited conceptual coverage (only nine target concepts).
Focus on GEMMA model family, may not generalize to newer models.
Regression formulation requires further refinement.
Label noise from LLM-based judges and qualitative nature of tasks.
papers.abstract: Activation-based steering enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to exhibit targeted behaviors by intervening on intermediate activations without retraining. Despite its widespread use, the mechanistic factors that govern when steering succeeds or fails remain poorly understood, as prior work has relied primarily on black-box outputs or LLM-based judges. In this study, we investigate whether the reliability of steering can be diagnosed using internal model signals. We focus on two information-theoretic measures: the entropy-derived Normalized Branching Factor (NBF), and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between steered activations and targeted concepts in the vocabulary space. We hypothesize that effective steering corresponds to structured entropy preservation and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps. Building on a reliability study demonstrating high inter-judge agreement between two architecturally distinct LLMs, we use LLM-generated annotations as ground truth and show that these mechanistic signals provide meaningful predictive power for identifying successful steering and estimating failure probability. We further introduce a stronger evaluation baseline for Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-based steering, the two most widely adopted activation-steering methods.

papers.title: FADE: Why Bad Descriptions Happen to Good Features
papers.research_question: How to develop a scalable, model-agnostic framework for automatically evaluating feature-to-description alignment in automated interpretability pipelines?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FADE, a framework for evaluating feature-to-description alignment with four metrics, and provides insights into challenges in automated interpretability.
papers.conclusion: FADE provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for feature descriptions, highlighting fundamental challenges in automated interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
FADE identifies limitations of single-metric approaches like simulated-activation-based metrics.
Larger evaluating LLMs yield better evaluations, with models like GPT-4o mini performing well.
Generating feature descriptions for SAEs is more challenging than for MLP neurons.
Interpreting larger SAEs is more difficult due to finer-grained concept decomposition.
Interpretability varies across layers, with some layers like layer 12 in Gemma-2-2b being less interpretable.
papers.limitation: The framework relies on assumptions such as binary concept expression, concept sparsity, feature reactivity, and causality, which may not always hold.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have highlighted the potential of automating interpretability pipelines in analyzing the latent representations within LLMs. While this may enhance our understanding of internal mechanisms, the field lacks standardized evaluation methods for assessing the validity of discovered features. We attempt to bridge this gap by introducing FADE: Feature Alignment to Description Evaluation, a scalable model-agnostic framework for automatically evaluating feature-to-description alignment. FADE evaluates alignment across four key metrics - Clarity, Responsiveness, Purity, and Faithfulness - and systematically quantifies the causes of the misalignment between features and their descriptions. We apply FADE to analyze existing open-source feature descriptions and assess key components of automated interpretability pipelines, aiming to enhance the quality of descriptions. Our findings highlight fundamental challenges in generating feature descriptions, particularly for SAEs compared to MLP neurons, providing insights into the limitations and future directions of automated interpretability. We release FADE as an open-source package at: https://github.com/brunibrun/FADE

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
